analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue police for misconduct, ends qualified immunity, and restricts racial profiling, chokeholds, and no-knock raids.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill was introduced in August 2024 with 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it easier to hold police officers accountable in court, most notably by ending qualified immunity — the legal shield that protects officers from lawsuits over misconduct. It would lower the bar for federal criminal charges against officers, ban racial profiling by law enforcement, ban no-knock warrants in drug cases and chokeholds (tying federal grant money to compliance), require federal officers to wear body cameras, create a national misconduct registry, and collect public data on traffic stops, use of force, and deaths. It was introduced in the final five months of the 118th Congress, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are stopped, searched, or subjected to force by police — disproportionately Black and Hispanic Americans — along with victims of police misconduct who currently cannot sue because of qualified immunity. Families of people killed by police would gain an independent-investigation pathway outside the local department, and the public would gain access to nationwide data on stops, force, and officer misconduct records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People policed, especially Black and Hispanic residents

how_it_helps.text: Strips qualified immunity so local and federal officers can be sued even if they reasonably but wrongly believed their conduct was legal, removing the most common reason courts throw out police misconduct lawsuits [S2].

Lowers the intent standard for the federal criminal civil-rights statute from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly,' making it easier to prosecute officers who violate someone's constitutional rights [S2].
Bans racial profiling by any law enforcement agent and lets individuals sue for injunctive relief, with proof of a disparate impact serving as prima facie evidence [S2].

Bans no-knock warrants in federal drug cases and withholds COPS grant money from states that allow them, and bans chokeholds and carotid holds for federal officers while conditioning Byrne and COPS grants on states doing the same [S2].

Creates a national registry of officer misconduct and decertification records, publicly accessible, and requires agencies to check it before hiring, with federal grant eligibility tied to compliance [S2].
Requires public federal reporting of all stops, searches, and use-of-force incidents broken down by race, ethnicity, age, and gender, and makes federal officers wear body cameras [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, which face new reporting duties, accreditation and training costs, and potential loss of federal grant money if they do not comply. Individual officers lose the qualified-immunity shield and would face more lawsuits and easier criminal exposure. Taxpayers fund roughly $880 million in new authorized grant spending over three years.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises civil and criminal liability for officers by ending qualified immunity and lowering the criminal intent standard; critics including police unions argued this would make it harder to recruit and retain officers and would make officers hesitant to act in dangerous situations [S2].

It ties federal law enforcement grants to state compliance on profiling bans, chokehold bans, no-knock bans, and training, which opponents view as federal overreach into state policing and a funding cut for jurisdictions that decline [S2].
Banning no-knock warrants in drug cases removes a tactic some agencies argue protects officers from ambush when serving warrants, trading officer safety for resident safety [S2].

The bill authorizes substantial new spending — including $750 million for independent investigation grants and $300 million for state pattern-and-practice investigations — adding to federal costs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real accountability for a government power that can end people's lives, and the main cost is higher legal and compliance costs for police agencies plus more lawsuits against individual officers. The design relies heavily on conditioning federal grants rather than direct mandates, which softens its effect on states that refuse. The strongest good-faith objection is that easier lawsuits and a lower criminal-intent standard could make recruitment harder and officers more cautious in violent encounters; supporters respond that the current rules shield misconduct at the cost of public trust and lives.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last five months of the Congress, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on August 1, 2024, with Sens. Durbin, Warnock, Padilla, Markey, Butler, Duckworth, and Hirono as original cosponsors [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the same day; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S1].
All 10 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored the bill [S3].
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and officer unions that opposed the reforms are better off; no officer will face the new liability, misconduct registry, or grant conditions, and no one will gain the new legal remedies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that would have faced the new rules

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act of 2024 on August 1, 2024, as the lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Warnock, Padilla, Markey, Butler, Duckworth, and Hirono
for.role: Original cosponsors (introduced the bill with Booker)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction [S2].

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but it never reached a vote, so their support never translated into floor action.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the Judiciary Committee from August 1, 2024 until the Congress ended, with no hearing or markup ever scheduled [S1].

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.role: Majority of the Senate at the time
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the previous version of this legislation had already failed in the Senate in 2021, making floor action untenable without their support.

against.name: National police unions (Fraternal Order of Police and police associations)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the earlier versions of the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, chiefly over ending qualified immunity and expanded liability, and were central to its 2021 failure; this 2024 version did not advance far enough for direct record engagement.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat (10 of 10), and the bill's earlier House-passed version in 2021 advanced almost entirely on Democratic votes, with Senate Republicans unable to reach a compromise — a fully partisan split with no recorded Republican support for this bill [S3].

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and officers' unions
industries.note: The bill removes qualified immunity, expands criminal exposure, requires misconduct reporting and decertification checks, and conditions federal grants on reforms. Its interest in stopping the bill runs against the public's interest in police accountability.

States and localities face new reporting, accreditation, and training duties and could lose Byrne and COPS grant money for noncompliance, but also could receive new grants for independent investigations and accreditation. They generally preferred no federal conditions on policing.

industries.industry: Law enforcement accreditation and body-camera vendors
industries.note: The bill pushes agencies toward accreditation from certified organizations and mandates federal body cameras and in-car recording, creating a customer base for those services and equipment.
